Today's cancer vaccine results from @moderna_tx and @Merck are exciting, confirming the earlier Phase 2 results and also the news we got a few months ago at @ASCO. 

They're also a great excuse to discuss the lifecycle of AI in the drug development process. 

All emerging technologies have a maturation lifecycle. AI  in the natural sciences is a perfect example.

On the "boring end", you have old-school ML classifiers, decision trees, SVMs, and computer vision techniques that are silently baked into every sequencing machine and molecular diagnostic workflow on the planet. Would you consider this "AI in drug development". 

No, you wouldn't. (1) Because precision diagnostics aren't drug development and (2) because these techniques don't get clustered alongside the frontier/hypey areas like 'virtual cell'. 

That's the other end of the spectrum, the "hypey end". 

These are the AI implementations that attract disproportionate venture investment, make all the headlines, and that have attached a bunch of very smart sounding reasons why they'll never work. 

They become associated with the whole. Folks will often point to them as class representatives for 'AI in drug development' as a simple way to reject the entire class's effects on the industry. 

I have an allergic reaction to this because, to me, data-driven/ML methods are inseparable from and massively contribute to the life sciences.

It's just that we don't celebrate the critical trailing edge because it's lost its sci-fi sheen, but it nonetheless serves as the foundation that all new advances become reality. 

So let's take the @moderna_tx and @Merck results. Would you consider this a success story for 'AI in drug development'? No, you probably wouldn't and I wouldn't blame you. 

It's true that cancer vaccines had/have many translational obstacles spanning delivery, supply chain, format, antigen selection, and more. It's foolish to try to decompose and assign credit to these pillars quantitatively. 

But let me zoom in to give some credit where it's due, because make no mistake, ML played a massive role.

Beyond the fact that advanced Illumina machines have onboard NVIDIA accelerators and run various deep-learning algorithms in their analysis pipelines, which provide the essential information for personalized cancer vaccines, I can offer up a few things you may not know. 

@PersonalisInc, the diagnostic partner for @Merck and @moderna_tx throughout these vaccine trials, spent years training ML algorithms on proprietary immunopeptidomics datasets (paired sequencing and mass-spec) to help with neoantigen presentation/immunogenicity prediction. 

This isn't commodity sequencing. These and other Personalis technologies enhanced by data-driven methods (e.g., enhanced HLA typing) were indispensable to this process by supplying the vaccine developers with high-fidelity mutanomes. 

We don't know everything about the handoff to Moderna (e.g. which models Personalis used versus Moderna used), but we do knew they used another algorithm in the pipeline to select the exact neoantigens to include in the vaccine formulation. 

So, I think it's safe to say that without the steady improvement in data-driven/ML/algorithmic techniques, we would not be standing here today with these results. 

Of course, we can wax poetic that 'these aren't neural networks', and you'd be making my point for me. These weren't leading edge AI implementations, which is why the fuller class of technology doesn't earn its roses here. 

But that's how this is going to happen. Non-leading AI techniques will continue creating value in drug development. Today's frontier techniques will improve, lose their association with 'hype', and folks will still move goalposts around what is AI in drug development. 

But that's the nice thing about goalpost moving. You can start to build a nice trend-line about where things are going. 

-------

*I use the term AI loosely to refer to all data-driven techniques. Don't @ me.

How to become an AI Engineer in 6 months 🚀

I just graduated with a CS degree and I'm living parts of this roadmap right now — sharing it because I wish someone had laid it out this clearly when I started.

**MONTH 1 — Foundations 🐍**
Learn: Python properly, NumPy + Pandas, SQL, Git/GitHub, APIs + JSON, Linux/CLI, linear algebra, probability + stats
Build: Data analysis project → ML API with FastAPI
Goal: Write production-ish Python, not just notebooks.

**MONTH 2 — Machine Learning 🧠**
Master: Linear/logistic regression, decision trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, KNN, clustering, feature engineering, train/val/test, cross-validation, precision/recall/F1/AUC, hyperparameter tuning
Learn: scikit-learn
Build: End-to-end ML prediction system
Goal: Understand WHY a model works, not just `.fit()`.

**MONTH 3 — Deep Learning 🔥**
Learn: Neural networks, backprop, activation/loss functions, optimizers, regularization, CNNs, sequence models, attention, transformers
Learn: PyTorch
Build: Image/text classification system

This is where CV clicked for me — I built FertLens, a computer vision system detecting fake fertilizer using MobileNetV3 with Grad-CAM heatmaps, as my final year project. 📱🌾

**MONTH 4 — LLM Engineering 🤖**
Tokens, embeddings, transformers, LLM APIs, prompting, structured outputs, function/tool calling, streaming, context windows, cost/latency optimization, Hugging Face
Then RAG: chunking → embeddings → vector databases → retrieval → reranking → grounded generation → evaluation
Build: 🔥 "Chat with your documents" — but don't stop at a basic chatbot.

**MONTH 5 — Agents + Production ⚙️**
Tool calling, agent loops, planning, memory, workflows, multi-step agents, guardrails, context engineering, MCP, orchestration (LangGraph or equivalent)
Build: 🔥 An autonomous research/automation agent
The skill isn't "using LangChain" — it's understanding the architecture underneath.

**MONTH 6 — Production AI Engineer 🚀**
FastAPI, Docker, cloud deployment, CI/CD, MLflow, logging, monitoring, evaluation, LLM observability, rate limiting, caching, auth, security, cost optimization

Deploy everything. Your GitHub should have:
1️⃣ Classical ML project
2️⃣ Deep learning project
3️⃣ Production RAG application
4️⃣ Agentic AI application

At least 2 should be genuinely impressive.

---

**EVERY WEEK**
30% Learning → 50% Building → 10% Papers/docs → 10% Interview prep
Code every day.

**THE INTERVIEW STACK 🎯**
DSA, OOP, DBMS, OS, Computer Networks, SQL, system design basics, Python
AI Engineer ≠ "person who knows ChatGPT." You still need to be an engineer.

**WHAT NOT TO DO ❌**
Don't collect 20 certificates, 50 prompt courses, 100 tutorials, copy-pasted repos.
Instead: Learn → Build → Break → Debug → Deploy → Explain. Repeat.

**THE END GOAL 🎯**
Train a model → build a neural net → understand Transformers → work with LLM APIs → build RAG → build agents → evaluate → deploy → monitor → explain your architecture in an interview.

That's the difference between "I know AI" and "I can build AI systems."

6 months is enough to be job-ready — not a research scientist. The roadmap is simple. The execution isn't. 🔥

10 Google search hacks you're sleeping on

if you're still Googling like it's 2015, here's what you're missing

1). master Google search operators

↳ "exact phrase" - pull exact word matches, no fuzzy nonsense
↳ site: - dig inside one specific website only
↳ filetype: - hunt down pdfs and docs directly
↳ -word - strip out results you don't want to see
↳ before:/after: - filter results by date

2). use Google AI mode

↳ research any topic without opening ten tabs
↳ compare your options side by side

↳ ask follow-up questions on the fly
↳ break down complex ideas way faster

3). search anything with Google lens

↳ identify random objects on the spot
↳ translate text just by pointing your camera
↳ find products you're eyeing in real life
↳ search straight from a screenshot
↳ get the full story on landmarks instantly

4). use circle to search

↳ circle it and google pulls up the info
↳ works on images, text, products, objects
↳ even works mid-video
↳ zero copy-paste, zero app switching
↳ never leave the app you're already in

5). find better results with filters

↳ date filters to cut old, irrelevant stuff
↳ exact keyword matching for precision
↳ news filters for real-time updates
↳ image filters to narrow visual search
↳ advanced search settings most people ignore

6). create Google alerts

↳ monitor your own name automatically
↳ track your brand mentions
↳ keep tabs on competitors
↳ follow entire industries hands-free
↳ catch trending topics before everyone else

7). reverse image search

↳ upload a photo and let google dig
↳ find the original source of any image

↳ track down products from a screenshot
↳ find a higher-quality version instantly

8). use Google instant tools

↳ set a timer straight from search
↳ run quick calculations
↳ check the weather in one search
↳ convert units or currency instantly
↳ get definitions and flight status too

9). learn faster with smart searches

↳ add "explain simply" to any search

↳ use "step-by-step roadmap" to learn faster
↳ turns google into your personal tutor

10). combine Google + Gemini

↳ pair search with ai for deeper research
↳ get quick summaries on demand
↳ plan your whole week in minutes
↳ brainstorm content ideas faster
↳ break down dense documents in seconds

MEET THE AI GIRL WHO PLAYS TENNIS FOR A LIVING — AND SHE'S NEVER LOST

She trains, competes, and racks up wins on camera. The catch: she doesn't exist.

Here's how the "AI athlete" model actually works:

An AI girl persona is built with a consistent face, body, and personality using image/video generation tools. Instead of lifestyle or fashion content, her niche is sport — match highlights, training vlogs, "behind the scenes" prep, rackets and outfits, rivalries with other AI athletes.

The mechanism is simple: physical talent doesn't need to be real, only the narrative around it does. Generated match clips, fake tournament brackets, and AI commentary create a storyline fans follow like a real career.

How she earns:

Sponsorship deals with sportswear/equipment brands looking for cheap, controllable "athletes"
Paid fan subscriptions for exclusive training content and match reactions
Licensing her face/likeness to sports betting or fantasy-sim apps
Selling a personal "AI coach" app trained on her persona
NFT/collectible drops tied to her "career milestones" (Grand Slam wins, rankings)

The twist: her fanbase doesn't care that she's never held a racket — they're not following an athlete, they're following a story that updates on schedule
